workloads.name: SAXPY (vector update)
workloads.what: Updates a long vector with y = a·x + y: almost pure memory traffic.

peak: Memory: NVIDIA V100 SXM2 datasheet: 900 GB/s HBM2
measured: Measured memory limit: 845 GB/s (94% of theory)
header.achieved: At sizes larger than the cache: 692 GB/s to 849 GB/s (77–94% of the theoretical limit); best at vector length 256M, fp32.
why: Each element is read and written once with almost no arithmetic, so memory speed sets the limit; sizes that fit in the cache can run faster than memory allows.

workloads.name: Sparse matrix × vector (SpMV)
workloads.what: Multiplies a matrix that is mostly zeros by a vector, as used in scientific solvers.

peak: Memory: NVIDIA V100 SXM2 datasheet: 900 GB/s HBM2

why: Mostly streams the matrix from memory; the irregular (power-law) matrix reads the vector at scattered places, which wastes part of the memory bandwidth.

workloads.name: Matrix multiply (GEMM)
workloads.what: Multiplies two dense square matrices: the core operation of scientific computing and AI.

peak: Compute: 80 SMs × 64 fp32 cores × 2 × 1.53 GHz boost = 15.7 TFLOP/s fp32; fp64 = half
measured: Measured compute limit: 14.1 TFLOP/s fp32 (90% of theory) · 7.0 TFLOP/s fp64 (90% of theory)
header.achieved: Reached 5.4 TFLOP/s to 14.0 TFLOP/s across sizes (69–93% of the theoretical limit); best at matrix size n 8K, fp32.
why: Matrix multiply reuses each value many times, so large matrices run close to the compute limit; small matrices are held back by start-up overhead.
The datasheet assumes a 1.53 GHz clock; under its power limit this GPU ran matrix multiply at about 1.39 GHz, which explains most of the gap to the datasheet.

workloads.name: Image convolution
workloads.what: Slides a small filter over a large image, as in image processing.

peak: Compute: 80 SMs × 64 fp32 cores × 2 × 1.53 GHz boost = 15.7 TFLOP/s fp32; fp64 = half
measured: Measured compute limit: 14.1 TFLOP/s fp32 (90% of theory) · 7.0 TFLOP/s fp64 (90% of theory)
header.achieved: Reached 10,779 Mpixels/s to 88,086 Mpixels/s across sizes (8–24% of the theoretical limit); best at image size 8K, 1 channel, 3×3 filter.
why: Small filters do little arithmetic per pixel, so only part of the compute limit is reachable; larger filters do more work per pixel and get closer.
Our own hand-written kernel is the fastest at almost every size on every machine: general-purpose neural-network libraries are not built for one small filter over a large image.

workloads.name: SHA-256 hashing
workloads.what: Computes SHA-256 fingerprints of many messages.

peak: No single hardware limit applies: speed is set by the hash rounds, so results are reported in GB/s.
header.achieved: Reached 51.9 GB/s to 105 GB/s across sizes; best at message length 1K, hardware crypto on.
why: Processors use their built-in SHA instructions; the GPU computes the hash in software. Short messages spend more time on per-message overhead.
Our GPU kernel reads each message separately; a layout that interleaves messages might be faster (not yet tested).

workloads.name: Histogram

workloads.name: Llama-3 inference
workloads.what: Runs a Llama-3 language model: processing a prompt and generating new tokens.

peak: Memory: NVIDIA V100 SXM2 datasheet: 900 GB/s HBM2
Compute: 80 SMs × 64 fp32 cores × 2 × 1.53 GHz boost = 15.7 TFLOP/s fp32; fp64 = half
measured: Measured memory limit: 845 GB/s (94% of theory)
Measured compute limit: 14.1 TFLOP/s fp32 (90% of theory) · 7.0 TFLOP/s fp64 (90% of theory)
header.achieved: Token generation: up to 679 tokens/s (66% of the theoretical memory limit at best); Prompt processing: up to 5,904 tokens/s (93% of the theoretical compute limit at best).
why: Generating each token reads all model weights from memory, so it is limited by memory speed; processing a prompt reuses the weights and is limited by compute.
Only the 1-billion-parameter model fits in this GPU's 16 GB; token generation is replayed as a single recorded GPU program to avoid launch overhead.
